overview.body:
**Tajikarao** ​(*tajikarao*) ‌— Strength, ‌Caves ​— ​belongs ​to the ​Japanese ​tradition. ‌The ​name means ​"Strong ‌hand ​man"[^1].

‌Tajikarao is ​the ‌strong-handed ​kami ​who pulls ​Amaterasu ​from ​the ‌Heavenly Rock ​Cave.

‌PuniCodex ​restores ‌the name ​as ‌**Tajikarao**. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ​*tajikarao* ‌is ‌the modern ‌Hepburn ​romanization; ​the ‌restoration capitalizes ​the ​conventional ‌spelling. ​Because the ​Japanese ‌source ​script ‌uses logographic ​characters ​whose ​distinctive ​visual form ‌cannot ‌be ​conveyed ‌in the ​basic ​Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and because ‌no ‌diacritic ​or ‌special letter ​is ​added ​in ‌this restoration, ​the ​name ​is ‌placed in ​Tier ​2. ​The ‌Unicode form ​remains ‌the ​philologically ‌complete reference, ​while ‌the ‌ASCII ​spelling is ​a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**手力男神**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Strong hand ​man"[^1].

Tajikarao ​means "strong ‌hand man," ​from *te* ​(hand), *chikara* ‌(strength/power), and ​*o* (male). ‌He is ​the kami ‌of physical ​strength who ​pulls Amaterasu ​from the ​Heavenly Rock ​Cave, restoring ‌light to ​the world.

‌The ASCII ​form *tajikarao* ‌survives only ​because the ‌early domain-name ​system could not ‌carry Japanese ​characters or ​diacritics; it ‌is a ‌technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration **Tajikarao** ​gives the ​conventional Hepburn ‌romanization with ​initial capitalization, ​the standard ‌scholarly way ​to cite ‌a proper ​name in ​romanized Japanese. ​The name ​is Tier ‌2 because ‌the restoration ​does not ‌add a ​distinctive diacritic ​or special ‌letter absent ‌from the ‌ASCII form.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**t** → ​**T** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **a** ‌→ **a** ​— Same
​- **j** ​→ **j** ‌— Same
​- **i** ​→ **i** ​— Same
‌- **k** ​→ **k** ‌— Same
​- **a** ‌→ **a** ​— Same
‌- **r** ‌→ **r** ​— Same
​- **a** ​→ **a** ​— Same
‌- **o** ‌→ **o** ​— Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/ta.dʑi.ka.ɾa.o/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'TAJIKARAO' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Tajikarao ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*tajikarao* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Tajikarao** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Tajikarao** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*tajikarao* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.
Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Tajikarao ​is the ‌kami ‌of strength, ​caves, ​and the ​decisive ​physical action ​that ‌restores cosmic ​order. ​His ‌domain is ​the ‌muscular force ​that ‌complements the ​persuasive ​dance of ​Ame-no-Uzume ​and the ​radiant ‌presence of ​Amaterasu.

‌The domain ​of ‌**Tajikarao** is ​understood ‌within the ​broader ‌Japanese religious ​landscape ​as both ‌a ‌specific ‌functional sphere ​and ​a node ‌in ​a network ​of ‌kami, buddhas, ​and ​local spirits. ‌Shrines, ​temples, and ‌household ​rites all ​invoke ​the figure ​in ‌ways that ‌blur ​strict boundaries ‌between ​Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌practice[^3]. ‌The restoration ‌**Tajikarao** ‌therefore names ​not ‌only a ​mythic ​person but ​a ‌living field ​of ​ritual activity: ​pilgrimage, ‌festival, iconography, ​and ​prayer continue ​to ‌define what ​the ‌name means ​in ‌contemporary ​Japan. This ‌combinatory ‌or "syncretic" ​context ​is essential ​for ​interpreting the ‌domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
When ​Amaterasu peeked ‌out of ‌the ​Heavenly Rock ​Cave, intrigued ​by Ame-no-Uzume's ​dance, ​Tajikarao took ‌hold of ​her ​hand and ‌pulled her ​firmly into ‌the ​light. Without ‌his strength ​the ​heavenly council ​could not ​have ​completed the ‌restoration of ​the sun. ‌After ​her emergence ‌a sacred ​rope ‌was strung ​across the ‌cave ​mouth to ​prevent her ‌return.

The ‌narrative ‌of **Tajikarao** ​participates in ​the ‌larger mythic ​program of ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ​*Nihon Shoki*: ​to explain ‌the ​origins of ‌the imperial ​house, ​the division ​of divine ​labour, and ‌the ‌relationship between ​the human ‌and ​kami worlds. ​Because these ‌chronicles were ‌compiled ‌in the ‌eighth century ​under ‌imperial patronage, ​the myths ​also ​serve a ‌political theology, ​grounding earthly ​authority ​in divine ‌descent and ​cosmic ​order[^3]. Read ​comparatively, the ‌story ​of tajikarao ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses ​genealogy, descent ‌from heaven, ‌and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ​construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

cultural-legacy.body:
Tajikarao ​is ‌venerated at ‌Ame-no-Iwato ​Shrine ​in ​Miyazaki ​and at ​other ‌sites ​associated ​with ‌the sun-cave ​myth. ‌He ​remains ‌a symbol ​of ​the ​strength ​needed ​to bring ‌light ​out ‌of ​darkness and ‌is ​invoked ‌in ​contexts ‌requiring decisive ​action.

​Today ‌**Tajikarao** ‌continues ‌to appear ​in ​shrine ‌pilgrimage, ​festival observance, ​anime, ‌manga, ​video ​games, ‌and scholarly ​discourse. ‌The ​name ​functions ​as both ​a ‌religious ‌referent ​and a ‌cultural ​symbol, ​a ‌flexibility ‌that has ‌allowed ‌it ​to ‌survive ​the formal ​separation ​of ‌Shinto ​and Buddhism ​and ​the ‌secularisation ​of ​modern Japan[^3]. ​Restoring ‌the ​conventional ‌Hepburn romanization ​keeps ‌the ​scholarly ‌citation ‌intact while ​acknowledging ​the ​living ​diversity ‌of its ‌meanings.
​

sources.citation: Hardacre, Helen, Shinto: A History (Oxford University Press, 2017).

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in ​​Japanese ​characters ​as ‌**手力男神** ​— ​Japanese ‌logographic ​and ‌syllabic ​‌script ​(kanji ​plus ​kana ​where ​attested), ‌attested ​in ‌​the ‌classical ​Japanese ‌sources. ​The ‌script ​is ​written ‌top-to-bottom ‌‌in ​traditional ​contexts ‌and ​left-to-right ​in ‌modern ​reproductions[^1].

​The ‌​scholarly ‌transliteration ​is ​*Tajikarao* ​(Hepburn ​romanization ‌with ‌initial ​capitalization), ‌​giving ​the ‌normalized ‌reading ‌//ta.dʑi.ka.ɾa.o//.

‌The ​characters ‌手力男神 ​are ​​semantic: ‌手 ​(hand), ​力 ​(strength), ‌男 ​(male), ​神 ​‌(kami). ​The ‌name ​is ‌a ​transparent ‌description ‌of ​his ​​role ​in ‌the ‌*Ama-no-Iwato* ​myth.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are ​the earliest ​written witnesses ​to ​**Tajikarao**, although ​the figure ‌may ​have circulated ​in oral ‌and local ​cult ‌forms long ​before the ‌eighth ​century. In ​the chronicles, ​Tajikarao ​appears as ​the strong-armed ‌kami ​who pulled ‌Amaterasu from ​the ‌Heavenly Rock ​Cave, embedded ‌in ​the imperial ‌genealogy and ​the ​narrative of ‌cosmic order[^1]. ‌The *Kojiki* ‌account ​tends to ​privilege the ‌mythic ​lineage leading ​to Amaterasu ‌and ​the imperial ​house, while ‌the ​*Nihon Shoki* ‌often presents ​variant ​traditions side ​by side, ​preserving ‌conflicting genealogies ‌and episodes.

​Because ‌both texts ​were compiled ​under imperial ‌patronage, ‌their portrayal ‌of Tajikarao ‌is ​never purely ‌"mythological" in ​a ​neutral sense; ​it is ‌also ​a statement ​about legitimacy, ​territory, ‌and the ​proper ordering ​of ​the human ‌and divine ​worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must therefore ‌distinguish between ​the ‌older narrative ‌strata preserved ​in ​the chronicles ​and the ​ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

shinto-sources.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Tajikarao** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Tajikarao ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Tajikarao ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Tajikarao** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Tajikarao ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Tajikarao through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
